newsitem.title: USA: Dlr closes lower in U.S. after mark surge.
newsitem.headline: Dlr closes lower in U.S. after mark surge.

text.p: The dollar ended lower as the mark continued to rally after a Bundesbank member spoke of a postponement in Europe's planned currency union.

The mark firmed against the pound and was strong in Europe after Bundesbank council member Klaus-Dieter Kuehbacher joined a number of German officials who this week seemed to throw cold water on the plan to merge Europe's currencies in 1999.

"It's a broad-based dollar sale, in combination with a broad-based advance of the deutschemark against its major trading partners," said John Nelson, foreign exchange trading manager at ABN-AMRO Bank.
The dollar touched 1.6718 marks and hit a low of 122.15 yen in the U.S. It ended at 1.6735/40 marks, down from 1.6820/30 at the open and at 122.42/47 yen, off slightly from 122.48/58.

In an interview with "Boerse Online" magazine published on Tuesday, Kuebacher said the single currency might have to be delayed because he saw little chance that Germany would be able to reduce its government deficit enough to meet the key condition for joining European Economic and Monetary Union -- a budget shortfall no larger than 3.0 percent of national output.

On Monday, German Finance Minister Theo Waigel sparked some mark buying when he told Germany's Bild newspaper, that strict adherence to the fiscal criteria for participating in the single currency was more important than the timetable.

Edgar Meister, another Bundesbank member, also sounded an uncompromising tone on Monday, saying the success of Europe's common currency largely depended on a stability-oriented interpretation of the various entry criteria.

Dollar/yen slipped in the U.S. on Tuesday, continuing the bout of yen profit-taking purchases started after Japanese Minister of Finance Hiroshi Mitsuzuka annouced that plans would be drawn up to aid Japan's troubled financial institutions, by improving land liquidity in Japan.

"If that comes true, then that only helps the Japanese economy, which in turn helps the Nikkei (225 stock index) rally and in turn the yen will strengthen," said Jeffrey Yu, a senior dealer at Sanwa Bank Ltd.
Sterling took the brunt of the mark's surge on Tuesday, as talk of EMU delay seemed to undermine its role as a haven from nervousness about forging one currency on the continent.
The U.K. unit was also pressured as the market continued to trim positions in preparation for a general election, which Prime Minister John Major announced on Monday would take place on May 1.

"It's not political jitters associated with the election so much, but I think it's more if there is going to be a delay in EMU ... then sterling as an alternative to EMU is not necessarily needed," said Bob Lynch, senior currency analyst at MMS International, a market consulting firm.

Sterling/mark dipped below 2.66 on Tuesday, but with the dollar so unsteady, the pound rose to $1.5903/10 from $1.5860/70 at the open. The dollar fell to 1.4385/95 Swiss from 1.4442/52 and it rose to Canadian $1.3732/37 from C$1.3730/35. The Australian dollar rose to $0.7878/83 from $0.7872/77.
